a code or codes of fair competition for the trade or industry or sub-
division thereof, represented by the applicant or applicants, if the 
President finds (1) that such associations or groups impose no 
inequitable restrictions on admission to membership therein and are 
truly representative of such trades or industries or subdivisions 
thereof, and (2) that such code or codes are not designed to pro-
mote monopolies or to eliminate or oppress small enterprises and will 
not operate to discriminate against them, and will tend to effectuate 
the policy of this title: Provided, That such code or codes shall not 
permit monopolies or monopolistic practices: Provided further, 
That where such code or codes affect the services and welfare of 
persons engaged in other steps of the economic process, nothing in 
this section shall deprive such persons of the right to be heard prior 
to approval by the President of such code or codes. The President 
may, as a condition of his approval of any such code, impose such 
conditions (including requirements for the making of reports and 
the keeping of accounts) for the protection of consumers, competi-

provisions of such code, as the President in his discretion deems 
necessary to effectuate the policy herein declared.
(b) After the President shall have approved any such code, the 
provisions of such code shall be the standards of fair competition 
for such trade or industry or subdivision thereof. Any violation of 
such standards in any transaction in or affecting interstate or foreign 
commerce shall be deemed an unfair method of competition in com-

amended; but nothing in this title shall be construed to impair the 
powers of the Federal Trade Commission under such Act, as 
amended.

invested with jurisdiction to prevent and restrain violations of any 
code of fair competition approved under this title; and it shall be 
the duty of the several district attorneys of the United States, in 
their respective districts, under the direction of the Attorney Gen-

violations.

operative_clauses.judgment_reason: Terminated by statutory repeal on 1935-06-14. The report command (paragraph 6) directs the Code Authority to submit to the Administrator a study of hours, rates of pay and conditions three months after the code's effective date, as a condition of the approval. The three-month period is a report deadline and is not an end; the command depends on the code and the Code Authority the code creates. The order states no period, condition or date of its own, so it has no own-terms end. Its operative effect depended on section 3 of Title I: under 3(b) the approved code's provisions became the standards of fair competition for the trade, a violation in or affecting interstate commerce was an unfair method of competition, under 3(c) the district courts could restrain violations and under 3(f) a violation was a misdemeanor. Section 2 of Senate Joint Resolution 113 (49 Stat. 375, chapter 246, approved June 14, 1935) provides 'All the provisions of Title I of such Act delegating power to the President to approve or prescribe codes of fair competition and providing for the enforcement of such codes are hereby repealed' and states no later effective date, so the approval's prospective operative effect ended when the resolution was approved. Actor: the Congress by Senate Joint Resolution 113. The date is the resolution's approval date, not a general rule's default: the repeal reaches this command because the command had legal effect only through the repealed provisions. June 16, 1935 is not an end (section 1 replaced that expiry with April 1, 1936). Schechter (May 27, 1935) is a validity characterization recorded in source_notes, not an end date.

original_representation.quote:
Whereas, the Secretary of Agriculture and the Administrator of the National Industrial Recovery Act having rendered their separate reports and recommendations and findings on the provisions of said Code, coming within their respective jurisdictions, as set forth in the Executive Order No. 6182 of June 26, 1933, as supplemented by Executive Order No. 6207 of July 21, 1933, Executive Order No. 6345 of October 20, 1933, and Executive Order No. 6551 of January 1934;

Now, Therefore, I, Franklin D. Roosevelt, President of the United States, pursuant to the authority vested in me by Title I of the National Industrial Recovery Act, approved June 16, 1933, and otherwise, do hereby find that;

1. An application has been duly made, pursuant to and in full compliance with the provisions of Title I of the National Industrial Recovery Act, approved June 16, 1933, for my approval of a Code of Fair Competition for the Linseed Oil Manufacturing Industry; and,

2. Due notice and opportunity for hearings to interested parties have been given pursuant to the provisions of the Act and regulations thereunder; and,

3. Hearings have been held upon said Code, pursuant to such notice and pursuant to the pertinent provisions of the Act and regulations thereunder; and,

4. Said Code of Fair Competition constitutes a Code of Fair Competition, as contemplated by the Act and complies in all respects with the pertinent provisions of the Act, including clauses (1) and (2) of subsection (a) of Section 3 of Title I of the Act; and

5. It appears, after due consideration, that said Code of Fair Competition will tend to effectuate the policy of Congress as declared in Section 1 of Title I of the Act; and,

6. Three months after the effective date of this Code, the Code Authority shall submit to the Administrator a study of the hours of labor, rates of pay, and other conditions of employment within this Industry, with the view of revising the wages, hours, and other conditions of employment as set forth in this Code.

Now, Therefore, I, Franklin D. Roosevelt, President of the United States, pursuant to the authority vested in me by Title I of the National Industrial Recovery Act, approved June 16, 1933, and otherwise, do hereby approve said Code of Fair Competition for the Linseed Oil Manufacturing Industry.

FRANKLIN D. ROOSEVELT

The White House,

April 20, 1934.

Clauses and sources are quoted from this registered file, not from the unregistered clause-drafts copy. Identity: number, date and subject agree across the APP page record, the census register ('Executive Order 6686—Approval of Code of Fair Competition for the Linseed Oil Manufacturing Industry', 1934-04-20) and the WPA 1944 numbered list (printed page 576: 'Code of Fair Competition for the Linseed Oil Manufac turing Industry approved.'). The recital names the report of the Secretary of Agriculture and of the Administrator under EO 6182 as supplemented; the register and WPA titles both name the approval of the Linseed Oil code. EO 6686 (April 20, 1934, Franklin D. Roosevelt) recites that the Secretary of Agriculture and the Administrator reported separately on the provisions within their respective jurisdictions, finds in five numbered paragraphs that the application, notice, hearings and statutory conditions were met, adds in paragraph 6 that 'Three months after the effective date of this Code, the Code Authority shall submit to the Administrator a study of the hours of labor, rates of pay, and other conditions of employment within this Industry', and in a final paragraph approves the Code of Fair Competition for the Linseed Oil Manufacturing Industry. The machine inventory was wrong (six clauses made of the findings; the approval omitted), so the inventory is corrected with two spans: the report command and the approval. Legal reading: both clauses depend on section 3. The approval has no period of its own. The report command is a condition of approval that section 3(a) expressly authorizes ('requirements for the making of reports'), addressed to the Code Authority the code creates; its three-month period is a deadline for a report, which under the owner's 2026-10-21 report-deadline ruling is not an end, and the code's effective date is not held, so the deadline could not be dated in any case. Both clauses end with the repeal on 1935-06-14.

source.quote:
No. 854. Argued May 2, 3, 1935.—Decided May 27, 1935.
1. Extraordinary conditions, such as an economic crisis, may call for 
extraordinary remedies, but they can not create or enlarge consti-
tutional power. P. 528.
2. Congress is not permitted by the Constitution to abdicate, or to 
transfer to others, the essential legislative functions with which 
it is vested. Art. I, § 1; Art. I, § 8, par. 18. Panama Refining Co. 
v. Ryan, 293 U. S. 388. P. 529.
3. Congress may leave to selected instrumentalities the making of 
subordinate rules within prescribed limits, and the determination 
of facts to which the policy, as declared by Congress, is to apply; 
but it must itself lay down the policies and establish standards. 
P. 530.
4. The delegation of legislative power sought to be made to the 
President by § 3 of the National Industrial Recovery Act of June 
16, 1933, is unconstitutional (pp. 529 et seq.); and the Act is 
also unconstitutional, as applied in this case, because it exceeds 
the power of Congress to regulate interstate commerce and invades 
the power reserved exclusively to the States (pp. 542 et seq.).

original_representation.quote:
An application having been duly made, pursuant to and in full compliance with the provisions of Title I of the National Industrial Recovery Act, approved June 16, 1933, for my approval of a Code of Fair Competition for the Canning Industry, and hearings having been held thereon and the Administrator having rendered his report containing an analysis of said Code of Fair Competition together with his recommendations and findings with respect thereto, and the Administrator having found that said Code of Fair Competition complies in all respects with the pertinent provisions of Title I of said Act and that the requirements of clauses (1) and (a) of subsection (a) of Section 3 of said Act have been met:

Now, Therefore, I, Franklin D. Roosevelt, President of the United States, pursuant to the authority vested in me by Title I of the National Industrial Recovery Act, approved June 16, 1933, and otherwise, do adopt and approve the report, recommendations and findings of the Administrator and do order that the said Code of Fair Competition be and it is hereby approved, subject to the following conditions:

(1) That the Industry shall designate a committee whose membership shall be subject to the approval of the Administrator and who shall cooperate with the Administrator in the formulation of standards of quality for products of the Industry and to make recommendations to the Administrator within ninety (90) days for the inclusion in said Code of provisions with respect to such standards and labelling requirements.

(a) That the Industry shall report not later than December 1, 1934 on the operation of the provisions of Articles III and IV with a view to improving the hour and wage provisions of this Code.

FRANKLIN D. ROOSEVELT

Approval Recommended:

     Hugh S Johnson

          Administrator.

The White House,

May 29, 1934.

source.quote:
No. 854. Argued May 2, 3, 1935.—Decided May 27, 1935.
1. Extraordinary conditions, such as an economic crisis, may call for 
extraordinary remedies, but they can not create or enlarge consti-
tutional power. P. 528.
2. Congress is not permitted by the Constitution to abdicate, or to 
transfer to others, the essential legislative functions with which 
it is vested. Art. I, § 1; Art. I, § 8, par. 18. Panama Refining Co. 
v. Ryan, 293 U. S. 388. P. 529.
3. Congress may leave to selected instrumentalities the making of 
subordinate rules within prescribed limits, and the determination 
of facts to which the policy, as declared by Congress, is to apply; 
but it must itself lay down the policies and establish standards. 
P. 530.
4. The delegation of legislative power sought to be made to the 
President by § 3 of the National Industrial Recovery Act of June 
16, 1933, is unconstitutional (pp. 529 et seq.); and the Act is 
also unconstitutional, as applied in this case, because it exceeds 
the power of Congress to regulate interstate commerce and invades 
the power reserved exclusively to the States (pp. 542 et seq.).

source.quote:
Sec . 3. (a) Upon the application to the President by one or more 
trade or industrial associations or groups, the President may approve 
a code or codes of fair competition for the trade or industry or sub-
division thereof, represented by the applicant or applicants, if the 
President finds (1) that such associations or groups impose no 
inequitable restrictions on admission to membership therein and are 
truly representative of such trades or industries or subdivisions 
thereof, and (2) that such code or codes are not designed to pro-
mote monopolies or to eliminate or oppress small enterprises and will 
not operate to discriminate against them, and will tend to effectuate 
the policy of this title: Provided, That such code or codes shall not 
permit monopolies or monopolistic practices: Provided further, 
That where such code or codes affect the services and welfare of 
persons engaged in other steps of the economic process, nothing in 
this section shall deprive such persons of the right to be heard prior 
to approval by the President of such code or codes. The President 
may, as a condition of his approval of any such code, impose such 
conditions (including requirements for the making of reports and 
the keeping of accounts) for the protection of consumers, competi-
tors, employees, and others, and in furtherance of the public inter-
est, and may provide such exceptions to and exemptions from the 
provisions of such code, as the President in his discretion deems 
necessary to effectuate the policy herein declared.
(b) After the President shall have approved any such code, the 
provisions of such code shall be the standards of fair competition 
for such trade or industry or subdivision thereof. Any violation of 
such standards in any transaction in or affecting interstate or foreign 
commerce shall be deemed an unfair method of competition in com-
merce within the meaning of the Federal Trade Commission Act, as 
amended; but nothing in this title shall be construed to impair the 
powers of the Federal Trade Commission under such Act, as 
amended.

operative_clauses.judgment_reason: Terminated by statutory repeal on 1935-06-14. The operative paragraph approves the amendments to the Code of Fair Competition for the Distilled Spirits Industry and modifies the previous approval to include approval of the code in its entirety as amended. The order states no period, condition or date of its own, so it has no own-terms end. Its operative effect depended on section 3 of Title I: under 3(b) the approved code's provisions became the standards of fair competition for the trade, a violation in or affecting interstate commerce was an unfair method of competition, under 3(c) the district courts could restrain violations and under 3(f) a violation was a misdemeanor. Section 2 of Senate Joint Resolution 113 (49 Stat. 375, chapter 246, approved June 14, 1935) provides 'All the provisions of Title I of such Act delegating power to the President to approve or prescribe codes of fair competition and providing for the enforcement of such codes are hereby repealed' and states no later effective date, so the approval's prospective operative effect ended when the resolution was approved. Actor: the Congress by Senate Joint Resolution 113. The date is the resolution's approval date, not a general rule's default: the repeal reaches this command because the command had legal effect only through the repealed provisions. June 16, 1935 is not an end (section 1 replaced that expiry with April 1, 1936). Schechter (May 27, 1935) is a validity characterization recorded in source_notes, not an end date.

original_representation.quote:
Whereas, the Federal Alcohol Control Administration has submitted for my approval, certain Amendments to the Code of Fair Competition for the Distilled Spirits Industry, and has rendered its report and recommendations and findings thereon:

Now, Therefore, I, Franklin D. Roosevelt, President of the United States, pursuant to the authority vested in me by Title I of the National Industrial Recovery Act, approved June 16, 1933, and otherwise, do hereby find:

1. That an application has been duly made, pursuant to and in full compliance with the provisions of the Act and of the Code of Fair Competition for the Distilled Spirits Industry, for my approval of Amendments to the said Code; and

2. That due notice and opportunity for hearing to interested parties have been given pursuant to the provisions of the Act and regulations thereunder; and

3. That hearings have been held upon the Amendments pursuant to such notice and the provisions of the Act and regulations thereunder; and

4. That said Code of Fair Competition as hereby amended will constitute a Code of Fair Competition as contemplated by the Act and complies in all respects with pertinent provisions of the Act, including Section 3 (a) of Title I thereof; and

5. That it appears, after due consideration, that said Code as hereby amended will tend to effectuate the policy of Congress as declared in Section 1 of Title I of the Act; and

Now, Therefore, I, Franklin D. Roosevelt, pursuant to the authority vested in me by Title I of the National Industrial Recovery Act, approved June 16, 1933, and otherwise, do hereby approve said Amendments and modify my previous approval of the Code of Fair Competition for the Distilled Spirits Industry by Executive Order dated November 26, 1933, to include an approval of said Code in its entirety as hereby amended.

FRANKLIN D. ROOSEVELT

The White House,

June 29, 1934.

source.quote:
No. 854. Argued May 2, 3, 1935.—Decided May 27, 1935.
1. Extraordinary conditions, such as an economic crisis, may call for 
extraordinary remedies, but they can not create or enlarge consti-
tutional power. P. 528.
2. Congress is not permitted by the Constitution to abdicate, or to 
transfer to others, the essential legislative functions with which 
it is vested. Art. I, § 1; Art. I, § 8, par. 18. Panama Refining Co. 
v. Ryan, 293 U. S. 388. P. 529.
3. Congress may leave to selected instrumentalities the making of 
subordinate rules within prescribed limits, and the determination 
of facts to which the policy, as declared by Congress, is to apply; 
but it must itself lay down the policies and establish standards. 
P. 530.
4. The delegation of legislative power sought to be made to the 
President by § 3 of the National Industrial Recovery Act of June 
16, 1933, is unconstitutional (pp. 529 et seq.); and the Act is 
also unconstitutional, as applied in this case, because it exceeds 
the power of Congress to regulate interstate commerce and invades 
the power reserved exclusively to the States (pp. 542 et seq.).

source.quote:
[CHAPTER 246.] JOINT RESOLUTION
To extend until April 1, 1936, certain provisions of Title I of the National Industrial Recovery Act, and for other purposes.
Resolved by the Senate and House of Representatives of the United 
States of America in Congress assembled, That section 2 (c) of Title I 
of the National Industrial Recovery Act is amended by striking out 
“ at the expiration of two years after the date of enactment of this 
Act ” and inserting in lieu thereof “ on April 1, 1936 ”.
Sec . 2. All the provisions of Title I of such Act delegating power 
to the President to approve or prescribe codes of fair competition and 
providing for the enforcement of such codes are hereby repealed: 
Provided, That the exemption provided in section 5 of such title 
shall extend only to agreements and action thereunder (1) putting 
into effect the requirements of section 7 (a), including minimum 
wages, maximum hours, and prohibition of child labor; and (2) pro-
hibiting unfair competitive practices which offend against existing 
law, including the antitrust laws, or which constitute unfair methods 
of competition under the Federal Trade Commission Act, as 
amended.
Approved, June 14, 1935.

operative_clauses.judgment_reason: Terminated by statutory repeal on 1935-06-14. The operative paragraph approves the amendments to the Code of Fair Competition for the Cotton Garment Industry and modifies the previous approval to include approval of the code in its entirety as amended, effective fourteen days after August 21, 1934 absent a contrary order, none of which is held. The order states no period, condition or date of its own, so it has no own-terms end. Its operative effect depended on section 3 of Title I: under 3(b) the approved code's provisions became the standards of fair competition for the trade, a violation in or affecting interstate commerce was an unfair method of competition, under 3(c) the district courts could restrain violations and under 3(f) a violation was a misdemeanor. Section 2 of Senate Joint Resolution 113 (49 Stat. 375, chapter 246, approved June 14, 1935) provides 'All the provisions of Title I of such Act delegating power to the President to approve or prescribe codes of fair competition and providing for the enforcement of such codes are hereby repealed' and states no later effective date, so the approval's prospective operative effect ended when the resolution was approved. Actor: the Congress by Senate Joint Resolution 113. The date is the resolution's approval date, not a general rule's default: the repeal reaches this command because the command had legal effect only through the repealed provisions. June 16, 1935 is not an end (section 1 replaced that expiry with April 1, 1936). Schechter (May 27, 1935) is a validity characterization recorded in source_notes, not an end date.

research_rationale:
Text and identity: EO 6828 is read in full in the registered American Presidency Project (APP) transcription jobs/app-executive-orders/output/texts/executive-order-6828-approving-amendments-code-fair-competition-for-the-cotton-garment.txt (grade mirror_transcription, acceptable_as_original false; standing note: original not yet held; replace and re-check quotes when an official copy is retrieved). Page check per jobs/claim-kit/AGENT_PROTOCOL.md (working-text paragraph), done 2026-10-29: the row with the same sha256 (62db0994c914...) in jobs/app-executive-orders/output/MIRROR_DOCUMENTS.jsonl is a common-crawl capture (CC-MAIN-2025-51, captured 2025-12-12T23:26:13Z, WARC location recorded so the page can be re-fetched) whose heading is 'Executive Order 6828—Approving Amendments to Code of Fair Competition For the Cotton Garment Industry' and whose date is 1934-08-21; that date agrees with the date line of the held text ('August 21, 1934.'), and the row's text_sha256 equals the held file's. The held file is the whole order (recital, operative paragraph, signature, the Administrator's recommendation and the date line); it carries no order number, so the number comes from the page record. Clauses and sources are quoted from this registered file, not from the unregistered clause-drafts copy. Identity: number, date and subject agree across the APP page record, the census register ('Executive Order 6828—Approving Amendments to Code of Fair Competition For the Cotton Garment Industry', 1934-08-21) and the WPA 1944 numbered list (printed page 589: 'Amendments to the Code of Fair Competition for the Cotton Garment Industry approved.'). The WPA list says the order approves amendments to the Cotton Garment Code (page 589). EO 6828 (August 21, 1934, Franklin D. Roosevelt) adopts the Administrator's report on hearings held on amendments to the Code of Fair Competition for the Cotton Garment Industry and orders 'that the said amendments be and they are hereby approved, and that a previous order of approval of said Code is hereby modified to include an approval of said Code in its entirety as amended, such approval to take effect fourteen (14) days from the date hereof' unless good cause to the contrary were shown to the Administrator before then and a subsequent order issued. Legal reading: one section 3(a) approval of amendments with a suspensive proviso. The proviso could have prevented the approval from taking effect on September 4, 1934 only through a subsequent order issued within the fourteen days; no held order concerning the Cotton Garment code issued between August 21 and September 4, 1934, and both EO 6861 and EO 6871 recite that EO 6828 'approved' the amendments, so the approval is treated as having taken effect on its terms. The approval has no period of its own and ends with the repeal on 1935-06-14. EO 6861 (September 28, 1934) stayed the effective date of the amendments to Articles III and IV, which by their terms were not to take effect until October 1, 1934, up to and including October 15, 1934; EO 6871 (October 12, 1934) revoked that stay's first paragraph, stayed the same amendments 'to and including December 1, 1934, after which date said amendments shall be in full force and effect', continued the committee and set further reports. Those are postponements of the effective date of part of what this order approved, not cancellations of the approval, and the amendments were to be in force after December 1, 1934; they are described here and are not cited as later events because the order's dossier carries no evidence record for them.

To summarize and conclude upon this point: Section 3 
of the Recovery Act is without precedent. It supplies no 
standards for any trade, industry or activity. It does not 
undertake to prescribe rules of conduct to be applied to 
particular states of fact determined by appropriate admin-
istrative procedure. Instead of prescribing rules of con-
duct, it authorizes the making of codes to prescribe them. 
For that legislative undertaking, § 3 sets up no standards, 
aside from the statement of the general aims of rehabili-
tation, correction and expansion described in section one. 
In view of the scope of that broad declaration, and of the

941.

source.quote:
No. 854. Argued May 2, 3, 1935.—Decided May 27, 1935.
1. Extraordinary conditions, such as an economic crisis, may call for 
extraordinary remedies, but they can not create or enlarge consti-
tutional power. P. 528.
2. Congress is not permitted by the Constitution to abdicate, or to 
transfer to others, the essential legislative functions with which 
it is vested. Art. I, § 1; Art. I, § 8, par. 18. Panama Refining Co. 
v. Ryan, 293 U. S. 388. P. 529.
3. Congress may leave to selected instrumentalities the making of 
subordinate rules within prescribed limits, and the determination 
of facts to which the policy, as declared by Congress, is to apply; 
but it must itself lay down the policies and establish standards. 
P. 530.
4. The delegation of legislative power sought to be made to the 
President by § 3 of the National Industrial Recovery Act of June 
16, 1933, is unconstitutional (pp. 529 et seq.); and the Act is 
also unconstitutional, as applied in this case, because it exceeds 
the power of Congress to regulate interstate commerce and invades 
the power reserved exclusively to the States (pp. 542 et seq.).

source.quote:
Sec . 3. (a) Upon the application to the President by one or more 
trade or industrial associations or groups, the President may approve 
a code or codes of fair competition for the trade or industry or sub-
division thereof, represented by the applicant or applicants, if the 
President finds (1) that such associations or groups impose no 
inequitable restrictions on admission to membership therein and are 
truly representative of such trades or industries or subdivisions 
thereof, and (2) that such code or codes are not designed to pro-
mote monopolies or to eliminate or oppress small enterprises and will 
not operate to discriminate against them, and will tend to effectuate 
the policy of this title: Provided, That such code or codes shall not 
permit monopolies or monopolistic practices: Provided further, 
That where such code or codes affect the services and welfare of 
persons engaged in other steps of the economic process, nothing in 
this section shall deprive such persons of the right to be heard prior 
to approval by the President of such code or codes. The President 
may, as a condition of his approval of any such code, impose such 
conditions (including requirements for the making of reports and 
the keeping of accounts) for the protection of consumers, competi-
tors, employees, and others, and in furtherance of the public inter-
est, and may provide such exceptions to and exemptions from the 
provisions of such code, as the President in his discretion deems 
necessary to effectuate the policy herein declared.
(b) After the President shall have approved any such code, the 
provisions of such code shall be the standards of fair competition 
for such trade or industry or subdivision thereof. Any violation of 
such standards in any transaction in or affecting interstate or foreign 
commerce shall be deemed an unfair method of competition in com-
merce within the meaning of the Federal Trade Commission Act, as 
amended; but nothing in this title shall be construed to impair the 
powers of the Federal Trade Commission under such Act, as 
amended.
(c) The several district courts of the United States are hereby 
invested with jurisdiction to prevent and restrain violations of any 
code of fair competition approved under this title; and it shall be 
the duty of the several district attorneys of the United States, in 
their respective districts, under the direction of the Attorney Gen-
eral, to institute proceedings in equity to prevent and restrain such 
violations.
(d) Upon his own motion, or if complaint is made to the President 
that abuses inimical to the public interest and contrary to the policy 
herein declared are prevalent in any trade or industry or subdivision 
thereof, and if no code of fair competition therefor has theretofore 
been approved by the President, the President, after such public 
notice and hearing as he shall specify, may prescribe and approve 
a code of fair competition for such trade or industry or subdivision 
thereof, which shall have the same effect as a code of fair compe-
tition approved by the President under subsection (a) of this section.
(e) On his own motion, or if any labor organization, or any trade 
or industrial organization, association, or group, which has complied 
with the provisions of this title, shall make complaint to the President

that any article or articles are being imported into the United States 
in substantial quantities or increasing ratio to domestic production 
of any competitive article or articles and on such terms or under 
such conditions as to render ineffective or seriously to endanger the 
maintenance of any code or agreement under this title, the President 
may cause an immediate investigation to be made by the United 
States Tariff Commission, which shall give precedence to investiga-
tions under this subsection, and if, after such investigation and such 
public notice and hearing as he shall specify, the President shall find 
the existence of such facts, he shall, in order to effectuate the policy 
of this title, direct that the article or articles concerned shall be 
permitted entry into the United States only upon such terms and 
conditions and subject to the payment of such fees and to such 
limitations in the total quantity which may be imported (in the 
course of any specified period or periods) as he shall find it necessary 
to prescribe in order that the entry thereof shall not render or tend 
to render ineffective any code or agreement made under this title. In 
order to enforce any limitations imposed on the total quantity of 
imports, in any specified period or periods, of any article or articles 
under this subsection, the President may forbid the importation of 
such article or articles unless the importer shall have first obtained 
from the Secretary of the Treasury a license pursuant to such regu-
lations as the President may prescribe. Upon information of any 
action by the President under this subsection the Secretary of the 
Treasury shall, through the proper officers, permit entry of the 
article or articles specified only upon such terms and conditions and 
subject to such fees, to such limitations in the quantity which may 
be imported, and to such requirements of license, as the President 
shall have directed. The decision of the President as to facts shall 
be conclusive. Any condition or limitation of entry under this sub-
section shall continue in effect until the President shall find and 
inform the Secretary of the Treasury that the conditions which led 
to the imposition of such condition or limitation upon entry no 
longer exists.
(f) When a code of fair competition has been approved or pre-
scribed by the President under this title, any violation of any pro-
vision thereof in any transaction in or affecting interstate or foreign 
commerce shall be a misdemeanor and upon conviction thereof an 
offender shall be fined not more than $500 for each offense, and each 
day such violation continues shall be deemed a separate offense.

original_representation.quote:
Whereas, Executive Order No. 6828 of August 21, 1934, approved, among other amendments of the Code of Fair Competition for the Cotton Garment Industry, amendments of Articles III and IV, which amendments by their terms are not to go into effect until October 1, 1934, and;

Whereas, a reorganization of the National Recovery Administration has just been effected and there are pending before the newly appointed National Industrial Recovery Board protests by the Cotton Garment Code Authority and by various members of the industry against said amendments to Articles III and IV, and it appears that said Board should have an adequate opportunity to investigate the facts and make its recommendations thereon, and;

Whereas, said protestants have stated that if an impartial committee were appointed to determine the issues involved in the protest, they would abide by its conclusions;

Now, Therefore, by virtue of and pursuant to the authority vested in me by Title I of the National Industrial Recovery Act of June 16, 1933 (c. 90, 48 Stat. 195), and in order to effectuate the purposes of said title, I hereby order:

1. That said amendments to Articles III and IV of the Code of Fair Competition for the Cotton Garment Industry be stayed up to and including October 15, 1934.

2. That the National Industrial Recovery Board shall forthwith appoint a committee of three impartial persons who have not heretofore formed an opinion concerning the subject matter of said amendments, which committee shall hear said protests, investigate the facts and report its recommendations on or before October 10, 1934.

3. That the National Industrial Recovery Board shall immediately transmit said recommendations to me.

This order is made upon the understanding that the protestants will accept as final and will abide by such decision and order as I shall make on or before October 15, 1934, after consideration of said recommendations.

FRANKLIN D. ROOSEVELT

The White House,

September 28, 1934.

The held file is the whole order (recital, operative paragraph, signature, the Administrator's recommendation and the date line); it carries no order number, so the number comes from the page record. Clauses and sources are quoted from this registered file, not from the unregistered clause-drafts copy. Identity: number, date and subject agree across the APP page record, the census register ('Executive Order 6861—Staying Certain Amendments to the Code of Fair Competition for the Cotton Garment Industry Approved by Executive Order No. 6828 of August 21, 1934', 1934-09-28) and the WPA 1944 numbered list (printed page 592: 'Effectivedate of amendments to ArticlesIII and IV of the Code of Fair Competition for the Cotton Garment Industry stayed untilOct. 15, 1934, and the National IndustrialRecovery Board ordered to appoint a committee of three to hear protestsagainst said amendments. XVII NRA Codes 523.'). The WPA list says the order stays the effective date of amendments to Articles III and IV of the Cotton Garment Code until October 15, 1934 and orders the Board to appoint a committee of three (XVII NRA Codes 523). The later order EO 6871 (the revoking order) is also page-checked: its APP page record (node 362578, common-crawl capture 2025-03-23) has the heading 'Executive Order 6871', date 1934-10-12 as in the text's date line, and a text_sha256 equal to the held file's. EO 6861 (September 28, 1934, Franklin D. Roosevelt), made 'in order to effectuate the purposes of said title', orders: (1) that the amendments to Articles III and IV of the Cotton Garment Code approved by EO 6828 'be stayed up to and including October 15, 1934'; (2) that the National Industrial Recovery Board 'shall forthwith appoint a committee of three impartial persons' who will 'hear said protests, investigate the facts and report its recommendations on or before October 10, 1934'; (3) that the Board 'shall immediately transmit said recommendations to me'. This is a mixed order, so each command has its own end. The machine inventory (a lead plus three items) is corrected to the three commands. Clause 1 (the stay): EO 6871 (October 12, 1934), paragraph 1, orders 'That paragraph numbered 1 of Executive Order No. 6861 ... be and it is hereby revoked.' The first end is that revocation on 1934-10-12, three days before the stay's own stated end (October 15, inclusive; exclusive reading: when October 15 began). EO 6871 paragraph 2 stays the same amendments to and including December 1, 1934; that is a separate new stay by the later order, recorded as a later event, not an extension of this stay (the stay and the revocation are express, so the strike-and-insert and further-exemption rulings do not turn the revocation into an amendment). Clause 2 (committee): EO 6871 recites that the Board 'pursuant to said Executive Order duly appointed Willard E. Hotchkiss, W. Jett Lauck and Donald M. Nelson ... as such committee, which said committee thereafter heard protests, investigated the facts and on October 10, 1934, did report its recommendations'. The command (appoint, hear, report by October 10) was performed and is exhausted on 1934-10-10, the date of the report; the appointment fell between September 28 and October 10. EO 6871 paragraph 3 continues the committee with new instructions on its own authority, which is a later event of the committee, not a continuation of this command. Clause 3 (transmittal): EO 6871 states that the President 'do[es] hereby approve and adopt the report and recommendations of said committee' on October 12, 1934, so the recommendations had reached him by then; the report was made on October 10. The transmittal was therefore made between October 10 and October 12, 1934. The exact day is not stated; the clause is dated 1934-10-12, the day by which the evidence shows performance, and the interval is stated. The order does not state that the Board itself carried the document, only that the recommendations had reached the President; that is the object of the command.

source.quote:
No. 854. Argued May 2, 3, 1935.—Decided May 27, 1935.
1. Extraordinary conditions, such as an economic crisis, may call for 
extraordinary remedies, but they can not create or enlarge consti-
tutional power. P. 528.
2. Congress is not permitted by the Constitution to abdicate, or to 
transfer to others, the essential legislative functions with which 
it is vested. Art. I, § 1; Art. I, § 8, par. 18. Panama Refining Co. 
v. Ryan, 293 U. S. 388. P. 529.
3. Congress may leave to selected instrumentalities the making of 
subordinate rules within prescribed limits, and the determination 
of facts to which the policy, as declared by Congress, is to apply; 
but it must itself lay down the policies and establish standards. 
P. 530.
4. The delegation of legislative power sought to be made to the 
President by § 3 of the National Industrial Recovery Act of June 
16, 1933, is unconstitutional (pp. 529 et seq.); and the Act is 
also unconstitutional, as applied in this case, because it exceeds 
the power of Congress to regulate interstate commerce and invades 
the power reserved exclusively to the States (pp. 542 et seq.).

Sec . 3. (a) Upon the application to the President by one or more 
trade or industrial associations or groups, the President may approve 
a code or codes of fair competition for the trade or industry or sub-
division thereof, represented by the applicant or applicants, if the 
President finds (1) that such associations or groups impose no 
inequitable restrictions on admission to membership therein and are 
truly representative of such trades or industries or subdivisions 
thereof, and (2) that such code or codes are not designed to pro-
mote monopolies or to eliminate or oppress small enterprises and will 
not operate to discriminate against them, and will tend to effectuate 
the policy of this title: Provided, That such code or codes shall not 
permit monopolies or monopolistic practices: Provided further, 
That where such code or codes affect the services and welfare of 
persons engaged in other steps of the economic process, nothing in 
this section shall deprive such persons of the right to be heard prior 
to approval by the President of such code or codes. The President 
may, as a condition of his approval of any such code, impose such 
conditions (including requirements for the making of reports and 
the keeping of accounts) for the protection of consumers, competi-
tors, employees, and others, and in furtherance of the public inter-
est, and may provide such exceptions to and exemptions from the 
provisions of such code, as the President in his discretion deems 
necessary to effectuate the policy herein declared.
(b) After the President shall have approved any such code, the 
provisions of such code shall be the standards of fair competition 
for such trade or industry or subdivision thereof. Any violation of 
such standards in any transaction in or affecting interstate or foreign 
commerce shall be deemed an unfair method of competition in com-
merce within the meaning of the Federal Trade Commission Act, as 
amended; but nothing in this title shall be construed to impair the 
powers of the Federal Trade Commission under such Act, as 
amended.
(c) The several district courts of the United States are hereby 
invested with jurisdiction to prevent and restrain violations of any 
code of fair competition approved under this title; and it shall be 
the duty of the several district attorneys of the United States, in 
their respective districts, under the direction of the Attorney Gen-
eral, to institute proceedings in equity to prevent and restrain such 
violations.
(d) Upon his own motion, or if complaint is made to the President 
that abuses inimical to the public interest and contrary to the policy 
herein declared are prevalent in any trade or industry or subdivision 
thereof, and if no code of fair competition therefor has theretofore 
been approved by the President, the President, after such public 
notice and hearing as he shall specify, may prescribe and approve 
a code of fair competition for such trade or industry or subdivision 
thereof, which shall have the same effect as a code of fair compe-
tition approved by the President under subsection (a) of this section.
(e) On his own motion, or if any labor organization, or any trade 
or industrial organization, association, or group, which has complied 
with the provisions of this title, shall make complaint to the President

(f) When a code of fair competition has been approved or pre-

[CHAPTER 246.] JOINT RESOLUTION
To extend until April 1, 1936, certain provisions of Title I of the National Industrial Recovery Act, and for other purposes.
Resolved by the Senate and House of Representatives of the United 
States of America in Congress assembled, That section 2 (c) of Title I 
of the National Industrial Recovery Act is amended by striking out 
“ at the expiration of two years after the date of enactment of this 
Act ” and inserting in lieu thereof “ on April 1, 1936 ”.
Sec . 2. All the provisions of Title I of such Act delegating power 
to the President to approve or prescribe codes of fair competition and 
providing for the enforcement of such codes are hereby repealed: 
Provided, That the exemption provided in section 5 of such title 
shall extend only to agreements and action thereunder (1) putting 
into effect the requirements of section 7 (a), including minimum 
wages, maximum hours, and prohibition of child labor; and (2) pro-
hibiting unfair competitive practices which offend against existing 
law, including the antitrust laws, or which constitute unfair methods 
of competition under the Federal Trade Commission Act, as 
amended.
Approved, June 14, 1935.

operative_clauses.judgment_reason: Terminated by statutory repeal on 1935-06-14. The operative order revises the fourth condition of the approval of the Code of Fair Competition for the Needlework Industry in Puerto Rico; the revised condition continues as part of that approval, amended, until the approval ends (owner ruling 2026-10-21, strike-and-insert). The order states no period, condition or date of its own, so it has no own-terms end. Its operative effect depended on section 3 of Title I: under 3(b) the approved code's provisions became the standards of fair competition for the trade, a violation in or affecting interstate commerce was an unfair method of competition, under 3(c) the district courts could restrain violations and under 3(f) a violation was a misdemeanor. Section 2 of Senate Joint Resolution 113 (49 Stat. 375, chapter 246, approved June 14, 1935) provides 'All the provisions of Title I of such Act delegating power to the President to approve or prescribe codes of fair competition and providing for the enforcement of such codes are hereby repealed' and states no later effective date, so the approval's prospective operative effect ended when the resolution was approved. Actor: the Congress by Senate Joint Resolution 113. The date is the resolution's approval date, not a general rule's default: the repeal reaches this command because the command had legal effect only through the repealed provisions. June 16, 1935 is not an end (section 1 replaced that expiry with April 1, 1936). Schechter (May 27, 1935) is a validity characterization recorded in source_notes, not an end date.

APPROVED CODE NO. 474—CODE OF FAIR COMPETITION FOR THE NEEDLEWORK INDUSTRY IN PUERTO RICO AS APPROVED ON JUNE 28, 1934

The Executive Order of June 28th approving the Code of Fair Competition for the Needlework Industry in Puerto Rico provided, in part in the fourth condition of approval, as follows:

"That there shall be appointed by the Administrator for Industrial Recovery, within ten days after the effective date hereof, a Puerto Rican Needlework Commission consisting of three persons: one of wdiom shall bo nominated by the Code Authority for the Needlework Industry in Puerto Rico, another of whom shall be nominated by the several Code Authorities of related industries in continental United States, and a third person to serve as chairman, shall be nominated by the National Recovery Administration."

It having been found by the National Industrial Recovery Board that the several Code Authorities of the related industries in the continental United States cannot agree upon a nominee for this Commission, and the said Board having recommended, in its report to me which is approved and attached hereto, a modification of the above-quoted provision.

Now, Therefore, I, Franklin Delano Roosevelt, President of the United States, pursuant to the authority vested in me by Title I of the National Industrial Recovery Act, approved June 16, 1933, and otherwise, do order that the abovequoted provision be and it is hereby revised to read as follows:

"That there shall be established a Puerto Rican Needlework Commission consisting of four members who shall be appointed by the National Industrial Recovery Board as follow's: one member to represent the Needlework Industry in Puerto Rico, on the nomination of the Code Authority for that industry, who shall have one vote; two members to represent the related industries in the continental United States, to be selected by the National Industrial Recovery Board from the nominations made by the Code Authorities for such industries, each of whom shall have one-half vote; one member to serve as impartial chairman, who shall have one vote."

FRANKLIN D. ROOSEVELT

Approval Recommended:

     The National Industrial Recovery Board

By G. A. Lynch,

     Administrative Officer

The White House,

Oct 11, 1934.

EO 6870-A (October 11, 1934, Franklin D. Roosevelt) recites the fourth condition of the June 28, 1934 approval of the Code of Fair Competition for the Needlework Industry in Puerto Rico (that the Administrator appoint, within ten days of the effective date, a three-person Puerto Rican Needlework Commission with members nominated by the Puerto Rican Code Authority, the continental related-industry Code Authorities and the National Recovery Administration), recites that the continental Code Authorities cannot agree upon a nominee and the Board recommended a modification, and orders that the quoted provision 'be and it is hereby revised to read as follows: ''That there shall be established a Puerto Rican Needlework Commission consisting of four members who shall be appointed by the National Industrial Recovery Board''' (one member for the Puerto Rican industry with one vote, two for the continental related industries with one-half vote each, and an impartial chairman with one vote). The machine inventory was a single clause starting inside the quotation of the old condition, so the inventory is corrected to two clauses: the revising order and the replacement condition with its appointment direction. Legal reading: both clauses modify a condition of a section 3(a) approval, which section 3(a) authorizes ('such conditions'). The Commission's only function, set out in the approving order, is to study the operation of the code against competing codes and recommend modifications of the code to the Administrator, and to recommend on piece rates; so the direction to appoint it has no operation independent of the code. Under the owner's 2026-10-21 strike-and-insert ruling the amended condition continues, amended, until the parent approval ends. No held record shows whether or when the Board appointed the four members; that is not needed for the end, because the Commission and the Board's duty to appoint it exist as a condition of the approval and have no object once the approval and enforcement provisions are repealed. If appointments were made earlier, that performance would not have ended the Commission's powers, which continued as part of the condition until the repeal on 1935-06-14.

source.quote:
No. 854. Argued May 2, 3, 1935.—Decided May 27, 1935.
1. Extraordinary conditions, such as an economic crisis, may call for 
extraordinary remedies, but they can not create or enlarge consti-
tutional power. P. 528.
2. Congress is not permitted by the Constitution to abdicate, or to 
transfer to others, the essential legislative functions with which 
it is vested. Art. I, § 1; Art. I, § 8, par. 18. Panama Refining Co. 
v. Ryan, 293 U. S. 388. P. 529.
3. Congress may leave to selected instrumentalities the making of 
subordinate rules within prescribed limits, and the determination 
of facts to which the policy, as declared by Congress, is to apply; 
but it must itself lay down the policies and establish standards. 
P. 530.
4. The delegation of legislative power sought to be made to the 
President by § 3 of the National Industrial Recovery Act of June 
16, 1933, is unconstitutional (pp. 529 et seq.); and the Act is 
also unconstitutional, as applied in this case, because it exceeds 
the power of Congress to regulate interstate commerce and invades 
the power reserved exclusively to the States (pp. 542 et seq.).

source.quote:
Sec . 3. (a) Upon the application to the President by one or more 
trade or industrial associations or groups, the President may approve 
a code or codes of fair competition for the trade or industry or sub-
division thereof, represented by the applicant or applicants, if the 
President finds (1) that such associations or groups impose no 
inequitable restrictions on admission to membership therein and are 
truly representative of such trades or industries or subdivisions 
thereof, and (2) that such code or codes are not designed to pro-
mote monopolies or to eliminate or oppress small enterprises and will 
not operate to discriminate against them, and will tend to effectuate 
the policy of this title: Provided, That such code or codes shall not 
permit monopolies or monopolistic practices: Provided further, 
That where such code or codes affect the services and welfare of 
persons engaged in other steps of the economic process, nothing in 
this section shall deprive such persons of the right to be heard prior 
to approval by the President of such code or codes. The President 
may, as a condition of his approval of any such code, impose such 
conditions (including requirements for the making of reports and 
the keeping of accounts) for the protection of consumers, competi-
tors, employees, and others, and in furtherance of the public inter-
est, and may provide such exceptions to and exemptions from the 
provisions of such code, as the President in his discretion deems 
necessary to effectuate the policy herein declared.
(b) After the President shall have approved any such code, the 
provisions of such code shall be the standards of fair competition 
for such trade or industry or subdivision thereof. Any violation of 
such standards in any transaction in or affecting interstate or foreign 
commerce shall be deemed an unfair method of competition in com-
merce within the meaning of the Federal Trade Commission Act, as 
amended; but nothing in this title shall be construed to impair the 
powers of the Federal Trade Commission under such Act, as 
amended.
(c) The several district courts of the United States are hereby 
invested with jurisdiction to prevent and restrain violations of any 
code of fair competition approved under this title; and it shall be 
the duty of the several district attorneys of the United States, in 
their respective districts, under the direction of the Attorney Gen-
eral, to institute proceedings in equity to prevent and restrain such 
violations.
(d) Upon his own motion, or if complaint is made to the President 
that abuses inimical to the public interest and contrary to the policy 
herein declared are prevalent in any trade or industry or subdivision 
thereof, and if no code of fair competition therefor has theretofore 
been approved by the President, the President, after such public 
notice and hearing as he shall specify, may prescribe and approve 
a code of fair competition for such trade or industry or subdivision 
thereof, which shall have the same effect as a code of fair compe-
tition approved by the President under subsection (a) of this section.
(e) On his own motion, or if any labor organization, or any trade 
or industrial organization, association, or group, which has complied 
with the provisions of this title, shall make complaint to the President

that any article or articles are being imported into the United States 
in substantial quantities or increasing ratio to domestic production 
of any competitive article or articles and on such terms or under 
such conditions as to render ineffective or seriously to endanger the 
maintenance of any code or agreement under this title, the President 
may cause an immediate investigation to be made by the United 
States Tariff Commission, which shall give precedence to investiga-
tions under this subsection, and if, after such investigation and such 
public notice and hearing as he shall specify, the President shall find 
the existence of such facts, he shall, in order to effectuate the policy 
of this title, direct that the article or articles concerned shall be 
permitted entry into the United States only upon such terms and

limitations in the total quantity which may be imported (in the

article or articles specified only upon such terms and conditions and 
subject to such fees, to such limitations in the quantity which may

be conclusive. Any condition or limitation of entry under this sub-

to the imposition of such condition or limitation upon entry no

(f) When a code of fair competition has been approved or pre-
scribed by the President under this title, any violation of any pro-
vision thereof in any transaction in or affecting interstate or foreign 
commerce shall be a misdemeanor and upon conviction thereof an

operative_clauses.judgment_reason: Terminated by statutory repeal on 1935-06-14. EO 6885-A (October 25, 1934, Franklin D. Roosevelt) incorporates by reference the annexed report of the National Industrial Recovery Board, finds that the amended code complies with Title I, orders 'that the Code as amended be and it is hereby approved' and modifies 'the previous approval of said Code ... to include an approval of said Code in its entirety as amended' (the Builders Supplies Trade code). The order states no period, condition or date of its own, so it has no own-terms end. Its operative effect depended on section 3 of Title I: under 3(b) the approved code's provisions became the standards of fair competition for the trade, a violation in or affecting interstate commerce was an unfair method of competition, under 3(c) the district courts could restrain violations and under 3(f) a violation was a misdemeanor. Section 2 of Senate Joint Resolution 113 (49 Stat. 375, chapter 246, approved June 14, 1935) provides 'All the provisions of Title I of such Act delegating power to the President to approve or prescribe codes of fair competition and providing for the enforcement of such codes are hereby repealed' and states no later effective date, so the approval's prospective operative effect ended when the resolution was approved. Actor: the Congress by Senate Joint Resolution 113. The date is the resolution's approval date, not a general rule's default: the repeal reaches this command because the command had legal effect only through the repealed provisions. June 16, 1935 is not an end (section 1 replaced that expiry with April 1, 1936). Schechter (May 27, 1935) is a validity characterization recorded in source_notes, not an end date.

Page check per jobs/claim-kit/AGENT_PROTOCOL.md (working-text paragraph), done 2026-10-29: the row with the same sha256 (ee86cd5cea00...) in jobs/app-executive-orders/output/MIRROR_DOCUMENTS.jsonl is a common-crawl capture (CC-MAIN-2025-47, captured 2025-11-14T21:11:16Z, WARC location recorded so the page can be re-fetched) whose heading is 'Executive Order 6885-A—Amended Code of Fair Competition for the Builders Supplies Trade' and whose date is 1934-10-25; that date agrees with the date line of the held text ('Oct 25, 1934.'), and the row's text_sha256 equals the held file's. The held file is the whole order (recital, operative paragraph, signature, the Administrator's recommendation and the date line); it carries no order number, so the number comes from the page record. Clauses and sources are quoted from this registered file, not from the unregistered clause-drafts copy. Identity: number, date and subject agree across the APP page record, the census register ('Executive Order 6885-A—Amended Code of Fair Competition for the Builders Supplies Trade', 1934-10-25) and the WPA 1944 numbered list (printed page 594: 'Amendments to Code of Fair Competition for the Build ers Supplies Trade approved. XVIII NRA Codes 313.'). The WPA list adds the citation XVIII NRA Codes 313. EO 6885-A (October 25, 1934, Franklin D. Roosevelt) incorporates by reference the annexed report of the National Industrial Recovery Board, finds that the amended code complies with Title I, orders 'that the Code as amended be and it is hereby approved' and modifies 'the previous approval of said Code ... to include an approval of said Code in its entirety as amended' (the Builders Supplies Trade code). Legal reading: a section 3(a) approval of a code of fair competition with no period, condition or exception of its own; its operative effect depended on section 3 of Title I and ended with the repeal of the approval and enforcement provisions on 1935-06-14 (Senate Joint Resolution 113, section 2), unless an earlier end appears. No earlier end was found (see the earlier-end check). 
Member checks: {"earlier_end_check":"No own-terms end: the order states no period, condition, 'until' date, 'pending' clause or provisional approval; its only operative command is the approval. The name search found one other order naming this code, EO 6312 of October 3, 1933, the earlier approval that this order modifies; an amendment of a code is a later event of the earlier approval, not an end of this order. No later held order names the code. Searches made on 2026-10-29: (1) a full-text search of every held order text numbered 6200 through 7100 under jobs/*/output/texts (APP, HathiTrust GPO, Wikisource and Federal Register texts; clause-drafts copies excluded) for the code's name; (2) a citation search of the same texts for this order's number; (3) a search of the same texts for general NRA orders that could suspend, cancel or supersede codes: the held general orders (EO 6354 as amended by EO 6710, EO 6646, 6711, 6750-C, 6764 and 6829) prescribe rules, contract terms and delegations, and none suspends, cancels or supersedes the code named here; (4) the census register titles (jobs/domesday-register/output/REGISTER.csv) and the WPA 1944 numbered list, read for this code's name; they show no cancellation, suspension or superseding code. Orders for which no text is held (for example EO 6454) could not be searched, so the search covers held texts only. No held record shows this code cancelled or modified under section 10(b), superseded by another code, revoked or suspended before June 14, 1935. June 16, 1935 is not an end: it was Title I's original two-year expiry under section 2(c), which section 1 of Senate Joint Resolution 113 replaced with April 1, 1936. The approved code's own text is not held (it is printed in the NRA Codes volumes the WPA list cites), so a code-internal expiry or effective-date term could not be read; no held order records one for this code. Schechter (295 U.S. 495, May 27, 1935) is recorded in source_notes as a validity characterization, not as an end date: it reversed one conviction and held the Live Poultry Code provisions invalid, it did not cancel or withdraw this approving order, and no held record shows this code cancelled or suspended on that date.","independent_command_check":"The order contains one command, the approval. It appoints no one, creates no body, delegates nothing under another statute and directs no agency. The recital that the Board 'rendered their report' is not a command to the Board.","savings_check":"Acts done and liabilities incurred under the code while the approval was in force are accrued effects, and the section 5 antitrust exemption for action complying with the approved code taken while Title I was in effect (and for sixty days after) is an accrued effect for that completed action. The proviso to section 2 of Senate Joint Resolution 113 narrows the exemption to agreements and action thereunder that put section 7(a) requirements into effect or prohibit practices already unlawful; it names agreements, states no time limit, and the held text does not settle whether it narrowed the exemption for action under codes before June 14, 1935. No held source shows a prosecution continued after June 14, 1935, and none continues the approval itself. This order states no savings or continuing clause of its own.","scope_check":"The inventory is one clause, the operative paragraph beginning 'Now, Therefore, I, Franklin D. Roosevelt' that adopts the Administrator's report and approves the code; the machine inventory is correct and is confirmed. The recital before it states the statutory findings on which the approval rests; the signature, the 'Approval recommended' line and the date line command nothing. The annexed report of the Board that the order incorporates by reference is not part of the held text; the operative command is the approval, and no condition, stay or exception appears in the order's own words. The approval is a single act of one scope; no partial event reaching only part of it was found."}

savings_residuals.reason: Acts done and liabilities incurred under the code while the approval was in force are accrued effects, and the section 5 antitrust exemption for action complying with the approved code taken while Title I was in effect (and for sixty days after) is an accrued effect for that completed action. The proviso to section 2 of Senate Joint Resolution 113 narrows the exemption to agreements and action thereunder that put section 7(a) requirements into effect or prohibit practices already unlawful; it names agreements, states no time limit, and the held text does not settle whether it narrowed the exemption for action under codes before June 14, 1935. No held source shows a prosecution continued after June 14, 1935, and none continues the approval itself. This order states no savings or continuing clause of its own.

To summarize and conclude upon this point: Section 3 
of the Recovery Act is without precedent. It supplies no 
standards for any trade, industry or activity. It does not 
undertake to prescribe rules of conduct to be applied to 
particular states of fact determined by appropriate admin-
istrative procedure. Instead of prescribing rules of con-
duct, it authorizes the making of codes to prescribe them. 
For that legislative undertaking, § 3 sets up no standards, 
aside from the statement of the general aims of rehabili-
tation, correction and expansion described in section one. 
In view of the scope of that broad declaration, and of the
17 Act of September 21, 1922, c. 356, Title III, § 315, 42 Stat. 858, 
941.

source.quote:
No. 854. Argued May 2, 3, 1935.—Decided May 27, 1935.
1. Extraordinary conditions, such as an economic crisis, may call for 
extraordinary remedies, but they can not create or enlarge consti-
tutional power. P. 528.
2. Congress is not permitted by the Constitution to abdicate, or to 
transfer to others, the essential legislative functions with which 
it is vested. Art. I, § 1; Art. I, § 8, par. 18. Panama Refining Co. 
v. Ryan, 293 U. S. 388. P. 529.
3. Congress may leave to selected instrumentalities the making of 
subordinate rules within prescribed limits, and the determination 
of facts to which the policy, as declared by Congress, is to apply; 
but it must itself lay down the policies and establish standards. 
P. 530.
4. The delegation of legislative power sought to be made to the 
President by § 3 of the National Industrial Recovery Act of June 
16, 1933, is unconstitutional (pp. 529 et seq.); and the Act is 
also unconstitutional, as applied in this case, because it exceeds 
the power of Congress to regulate interstate commerce and invades 
the power reserved exclusively to the States (pp. 542 et seq.).

source.quote:
Sec . 3. (a) Upon the application to the President by one or more 
trade or industrial associations or groups, the President may approve 
a code or codes of fair competition for the trade or industry or sub-
division thereof, represented by the applicant or applicants, if the 
President finds (1) that such associations or groups impose no 
inequitable restrictions on admission to membership therein and are 
truly representative of such trades or industries or subdivisions 
thereof, and (2) that such code or codes are not designed to pro-
mote monopolies or to eliminate or oppress small enterprises and will 
not operate to discriminate against them, and will tend to effectuate 
the policy of this title: Provided, That such code or codes shall not 
permit monopolies or monopolistic practices: Provided further, 
That where such code or codes affect the services and welfare of 
persons engaged in other steps of the economic process, nothing in 
this section shall deprive such persons of the right to be heard prior 
to approval by the President of such code or codes. The President 
may, as a condition of his approval of any such code, impose such 
conditions (including requirements for the making of reports and 
the keeping of accounts) for the protection of consumers, competi-
tors, employees, and others, and in furtherance of the public inter-
est, and may provide such exceptions to and exemptions from the 
provisions of such code, as the President in his discretion deems 
necessary to effectuate the policy herein declared.
(b) After the President shall have approved any such code, the 
provisions of such code shall be the standards of fair competition 
for such trade or industry or subdivision thereof. Any violation of 
such standards in any transaction in or affecting interstate or foreign 
commerce shall be deemed an unfair method of competition in com-
merce within the meaning of the Federal Trade Commission Act, as 
amended; but nothing in this title shall be construed to impair the 
powers of the Federal Trade Commission under such Act, as 
amended.
(c) The several district courts of the United States are hereby 
invested with jurisdiction to prevent and restrain violations of any 
code of fair competition approved under this title; and it shall be 
the duty of the several district attorneys of the United States, in 
their respective districts, under the direction of the Attorney Gen-
eral, to institute proceedings in equity to prevent and restrain such 
violations.
(d) Upon his own motion, or if complaint is made to the President 
that abuses inimical to the public interest and contrary to the policy 
herein declared are prevalent in any trade or industry or subdivision 
thereof, and if no code of fair competition therefor has theretofore 
been approved by the President, the President, after such public 
notice and hearing as he shall specify, may prescribe and approve 
a code of fair competition for such trade or industry or subdivision 
thereof, which shall have the same effect as a code of fair compe-
tition approved by the President under subsection (a) of this section.
(e) On his own motion, or if any labor organization, or any trade 
or industrial organization, association, or group, which has complied 
with the provisions of this title, shall make complaint to the President

that any article or articles are being imported into the United States 
in substantial quantities or increasing ratio to domestic production 
of any competitive article or articles and on such terms or under

may cause an immediate investigation to be made by the United 
States Tariff Commission, which shall give precedence to investiga-
tions under this subsection, and if, after such investigation and such 
public notice and hearing as he shall specify, the President shall find 
the existence of such facts, he shall, in order to effectuate the policy 
of this title, direct that the article or articles concerned shall be 
permitted entry into the United States only upon such terms and 
conditions and subject to the payment of such fees and to such 
limitations in the total quantity which may be imported (in the 
course of any specified period or periods) as he shall find it necessary 
to prescribe in order that the entry thereof shall not render or tend 
to render ineffective any code or agreement made under this title. In 
order to enforce any limitations imposed on the total quantity of 
imports, in any specified period or periods, of any article or articles 
under this subsection, the President may forbid the importation of 
such article or articles unless the importer shall have first obtained 
from the Secretary of the Treasury a license pursuant to such regu-
lations as the President may prescribe. Upon information of any 
action by the President under this subsection the Secretary of the 
Treasury shall, through the proper officers, permit entry of the 
article or articles specified only upon such terms and conditions and 
subject to such fees, to such limitations in the quantity which may 
be imported, and to such requirements of license, as the President 
shall have directed. The decision of the President as to facts shall 
be conclusive. Any condition or limitation of entry under this sub-
section shall continue in effect until the President shall find and 
inform the Secretary of the Treasury that the conditions which led 
to the imposition of such condition or limitation upon entry no 
longer exists.
(f) When a code of fair competition has been approved or pre-
scribed by the President under this title, any violation of any pro-
vision thereof in any transaction in or affecting interstate or foreign 
commerce shall be a misdemeanor and upon conviction thereof an 
offender shall be fined not more than $500 for each offense, and each 
day such violation continues shall be deemed a separate offense.

(c) This title shall cease to be in effect and any agencies established 
hereunder shall cease to exist at the expiration of two years after 
the date of enactment of this Act, or sooner if the President shall 
by proclamation or the Congress shall by joint resolution declare 
that the emergency recognized by section 1 has ended.

[CHAPTER 246.] JOINT RESOLUTION
To extend until April 1, 1936, certain provisions of Title I of the National Industrial Recovery Act, and for other purposes.
Resolved by the Senate and House of Representatives of the United 
States of America in Congress assembled, That section 2 (c) of Title I 
of the National Industrial Recovery Act is amended by striking out 
“ at the expiration of two years after the date of enactment of this 
Act ” and inserting in lieu thereof “ on April 1, 1936 ”.
Sec . 2. All the provisions of Title I of such Act delegating power 
to the President to approve or prescribe codes of fair competition and 
providing for the enforcement of such codes are hereby repealed: 
Provided, That the exemption provided in section 5 of such title 
shall extend only to agreements and action thereunder (1) putting 
into effect the requirements of section 7 (a), including minimum 
wages, maximum hours, and prohibition of child labor; and (2) pro-
hibiting unfair competitive practices which offend against existing 
law, including the antitrust laws, or which constitute unfair methods 
of competition under the Federal Trade Commission Act, as 
amended.
Approved, June 14, 1935.
